rows.name: US Dollar
_rating_cap_reasons: Base currency — all signals are measured against it

gates.name: Valuation: REER Z-Score
gates.label: REER Z-Score
gates.tip: Where the real effective exchange rate sits in its own 20-year distribution, in standard deviations. Negative is cheap. Normalising by each currency’s own volatility is what makes −1.5 mean the same thing for CHF as for TRY, which a raw percentage gap would not. Double-weighted — this is the model’s primary thesis.

gates.name: Valuation: REER vs 10y
gates.label: REER vs 10y
gates.tip: The current real exchange rate against its own 10-year average. −20% means it buys a fifth less abroad than its decade norm. Answers “how far”, where the z-score answers “how unusual”.

gates.name: Valuation: REER vs 5y
gates.label: REER vs 5y
gates.tip: The same measure over five years. Not redundant with the 10-year reading: the two disagree exactly when a currency’s regime has shifted within the decade, and that disagreement is itself a signal.

gates.name: Carry: Real Carry
gates.label: Real Carry
gates.tip: This currency’s real policy rate minus the US dollar’s. Double-weighted over nominal carry on purpose: ranking on nominal alone puts every high-inflation currency at the top of the book, which is the classic way carry trades lose money.

gates.name: Carry: Nominal Carry
gates.label: Nom. Carry
gates.tip: The policy-rate differential against USD, before inflation. What the position pays in nominal terms — informative, but on its own a trap.

gates.name: Carry: Real Rate
gates.label: Real Rate
gates.tip: Policy rate minus annual CPI inflation. A 37% rate against 35% inflation is roughly break-even, not a 37% yield.

gates.name: Carry: Carry/Vol
gates.label: Carry/Vol
gates.tip: Carry per unit of realised volatility. Four points of carry on a 6%-volatility currency is a different proposition from four points on a 25% one. Scored by rank within the universe rather than a fixed scale, because “good” depends on the volatility regime of the moment.

gates.name: External: Current Account
gates.label: Curr. Acct
gates.tip: The current account balance as a share of GDP; positive is a surplus. The best single summary of whether a country can fund itself without selling its own currency.

gates.name: External: Reserves Cover
gates.label: Reserves
gates.tip: FX reserves expressed as months of import cover. Three months is the conventional adequacy floor.

gates.name: External: Inflation Gap
gates.label: Infl. Gap
gates.tip: Distance outside the 1–3% target band, in percentage points. Scored as a gap rather than a level so that deflation is penalised like inflation — on a raw reading, a deflating economy would screen as maximally price-stable.

gates.name: External: GDP Growth
gates.label: GDP Growth
gates.tip: Annual real GDP growth. Slow-moving and one to two years stale by construction, so this pillar acts as a solvency filter rather than a timing signal.

gates.name: Momentum: 12m-1m
gates.label: 12m-1m
gates.tip: The twelve-month return against USD, excluding the most recent month. The skip is deliberate: one-month FX moves tend to reverse while three-to-twelve-month moves tend to continue, and blending the two blunts both.

gates.name: Momentum: 3m Return
gates.label: 3m Return
gates.tip: Spot return against the US dollar over roughly three months. Positive means the currency appreciated.

gates.name: Momentum: vs 200d MA
gates.label: vs 200d MA
gates.tip: Spot against its own 200-day moving average. Above zero is trading above trend.

gates.name: Momentum: REER Trend
gates.label: REER Trend
gates.tip: Six-month change in the real effective exchange rate. Nominal spot can drift on an inflation differential alone; a rising REER means real purchasing power is genuinely improving.

gates.name: Stability: Volatility
gates.label: Volatility
gates.tip: Annualised standard deviation of daily log returns over one year. The scoring range is calibrated to this universe’s observed 4–12% span rather than textbook extremes — a wider range compressed every currency into the same score and made the pillar a constant offset.

gates.name: Stability: Max Drawdown
gates.label: Max DD
gates.tip: The largest peak-to-trough fall against USD over three years. Catches what volatility misses: a managed crawl posts very low volatility while still losing a great deal of ground.

gates.name: Stability: Vol Regime
gates.label: Vol Regime
gates.tip: Three-month volatility divided by one-year. Above 1 means the currency is more turbulent than its own baseline — an early warning that fires months before annual macro data would show anything.

gates.name: Stability: Inflation Vol
gates.label: Infl. Vol
gates.tip: Standard deviation of the annual inflation series. Persistent price instability, which is a different fact from the current inflation level scored in the External pillar.

categories.name: Valuation
categories.tip: Is the real exchange rate cheap against its own history? The heaviest pillar, because mean reversion in the real exchange rate is the best-evidenced medium-horizon effect in FX — and because it rests entirely on BIS REER, the most reliable source in the project.

categories.name: Carry
categories.tip: What does holding this currency pay, net of inflation? Reliable positive expectancy with a fat left tail, which is why real carry outweighs nominal carry inside the pillar.

categories.name: External
categories.tip: Can the country fund itself without depreciating? Annual data, one to two years stale by construction — a solvency filter rather than a timing signal.

categories.name: Momentum
categories.tip: Has the repricing started? Deliberately light: momentum is a confirmation overlay on valuation, not an independent thesis.

categories.name: Stability
categories.tip: What the position costs in risk. Light because it is partly double-counted inside carry-to-vol, and because pegs — which would otherwise sweep it — are masked out of its market-risk gates.

ui.composite: The weighted average of the five pillar scores, over the pillars that apply to this currency. The denominator renormalises, so a pillar dropping out rescales the rest instead of dragging the score to zero.
ui.rating: LONG ≥ 57, LEAN LONG ≥ 39, NEUTRAL ≥ 25, otherwise AVOID — then capped. Thresholds are provisional: they are set on the composite’s natural scale, not yet calibrated against forward returns.
ui.gates: Gates passed out of gates that apply. The denominator varies by currency because structurally inapplicable gates are excluded from it — a peg is not failed for having no volatility signal.
ui.coverage: The share of applicable gates that actually had data. Below 25% the composite is an artifact of what happened to be missing, and the rating is capped at NEUTRAL.
ui.regime: float — freely floating, every gate applies. managed — heavily leaned against, gates still apply. peg — hard peg or currency board: valuation and market-risk gates describe the anchor, not this currency, so they are switched off and the rating is capped.
ui.na: Grey means not applicable, and there are two kinds. Structurally inapplicable gates leave both the numerator and the denominator, so the pillar renormalises. Missing data scores zero and stays in the denominator, so sparse coverage remains penalised.
ui.spark: US dollars per unit of this currency, sampled weekly over ten years. Rising means the currency strengthened against the dollar.
ui.policy_rate: The central bank’s policy rate, from BIS. Shown as a level; what the model actually scores is the differential against USD, and the same rate net of inflation.
ui.inflation_pct: Latest annual CPI inflation, from the World Bank. Annual data, so it lags the monthly policy rate it is subtracted from — a real-rate reading here mixes vintages.
ui.name: Click any row for the full metric breakdown: every gate with its value and score, the ten-year price history, and any rating caps.
